headline: DOJ asks D.C. Circuit to deny stay of DEA's 29 November cannabis rule
dek: The Justice Department told the D.C. Circuit on 23 November that DEA's 29 November rule is old law, citing 7,100 timely applicants.
key_points: The Justice Department filed a combined opposition on 23 November asking the D.C. Circuit to deny emergency stays sought by seven medical cannabis companies in cases 26-1324 and 26-1325.
The government argues DEA's 30 October letter only restated existing law, is not a final decision the court can review, and caused the companies no injury of its own.
A DEA declaration says about 7,100 registration applications arrived in the 60-day window, about 2,800 of them from Arizona, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania and Utah.
The companies' replies are due at 4 p.m. Eastern on 24 November; without a stay, the supply-chain limits apply from 29 November.
body: The Justice Department has asked a federal appeals court to let the Drug Enforcement Administration's 29 November supply-chain deadline for medical cannabis stand. In a combined opposition filed on 23 November in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, government lawyers said the seven state-licensed companies challenging the deadline are, in effect, asking for permission to buy and sell a controlled substance without federal authorization, and that their motions should be denied.

The filing answers two consolidated petitions, Standard Wellness Utah v. DEA (No. 26-1324) and G.P.M.II v. DEA (No. 26-1325), which we covered on 20 and 21 November. A three-judge panel of Judges Neomi Rao, Justin Walker and Bradley Garcia had ordered the government to respond by 4 p.m. Eastern on 23 November, The Marijuana Herald reported. The companies may reply by 4 p.m. Eastern on 24 November. No ruling had been issued when this edition went out.
## What the government told the court

The core of the brief is that nothing changed on 30 October. On that day DEA emailed an information letter to companies that had filed complete registration applications in the 60-day window after the 28 April rescheduling order. The letter said that, from 29 November, those applicants may only buy from and sell to other registrants or other timely applicants. The companies call that a new rule imposed without rulemaking. The government calls it a summary of what the Controlled Substances Act has always required.

Its reasoning runs through the closed system the Act creates: every manufacturer, distributor and dispenser of a controlled substance must be registered, and registrants may deal only with each other. The April order, the brief says, granted a limited exception that let early applicants operate as if registered while DEA reviews their files, as long as they also follow their state licence. It did not, in the government's reading, let anyone else into the chain, and it did not let early applicants trade with businesses that never applied in time.

The government also raises two threshold objections. First, it says the 30 October letter is not a final decision under 21 U.S.C. section 877, the provision that gives the D.C. Circuit jurisdiction over DEA actions, because it consummates no decision and creates no new legal consequence. Second, it says the companies lack standing for the same reason: if their obligations come from the statute and regulations, the letter did not cause their harm.
> The government's case rests on one claim: 29 November is not a new rule but the end of a grace period. If the panel accepts that framing, the stay motions have little left to stand on.
## The numbers DEA put on the record

The brief cites a declaration from DEA staff coordinator Megan Almendinger. According to the Herald's account of it, the agency received about 7,100 applications in the early window: roughly 4,300 for dispensaries, 2,100 for manufacturers and 700 for distributors. About 2,800 came from the four states in the lawsuits, Arizona, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania and Utah, including about 1,250 manufacturer, 1,200 dispensary and 350 distributor applications. DEA acknowledges it is still processing applications; the April order had asked it to try to finish reviews within six months.

The government uses those counts against the companies. If more than 7,000 businesses, thousands of them in the petitioners' home states, filed on time, the brief argues, then a compliant supply chain of early applicants is possible, and the companies have not shown any legal barrier to building one.

On our arithmetic from the same figures, the four petitioner states account for about 39% of all early applications and about 60% of early manufacturer applications. That cuts both ways. It supports DEA's point that compliant partners exist in those states. It also shows how much of the national medical supply chain sits in exactly the markets where the companies say the deadline will cause the most disruption.
## Who is asking for the stay

The first petition, filed on 18 November, comes from Standard Wellness Utah, Verde Americano and NW Confections OK 241AA, operating in Utah, Arizona and Oklahoma. According to the Herald, their filings say Verde Americano could lose about $600,000 a month in revenue and lay off about 95 of its 136 employees, Standard Wellness Utah puts affected sales at about $275,900 a month, and NW Confections says losing 15 dispensary customers could threaten its survival.

The second, filed on 19 November, comes from four Pennsylvania companies: G.P.M.II, MLH Explorations, Tri-Mountain Pure and Story of PA CR. Their problem is a split registration. Their dispensaries applied in the window; their cultivation and processing sites did not. They say DEA's application system caused that gap, and that the deadline could stop their own manufacturing arms from supplying their own stores.

The government's answer to the harm claims is blunt. The brief says the companies have no reliance interest in violating federal law, that harms flowing from how they set up their operations are self-inflicted, and that some petitioners never filed a timely application at all. It adds that a stay would interfere with DEA's administration of the Act and with U.S. obligations under the 1961 Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs.
## What it means for operators

For medical operators outside the lawsuit, the brief is the clearest statement yet of how the government reads the rules. Three points stand out. Registration is assessed per activity and per site, so a vertically integrated group can be inside the system at the counter and outside it at the grow. The 30 October letter is described as a promise not to enforce before 29 November, not a new duty starting on that date. And the government says that even a fully registered business could not buy from an unregistered one, which means the problem does not go away when DEA grants pending applications.

The filing also notes that a separate challenge to the rescheduling order itself, SAM, Inc. v. U.S. Department of Justice, is pending before the same court. That case could reshape the whole framework, but it runs on a separate track from the stay motions.
## What to watch

The companies' replies are due at 4 p.m. Eastern on 24 November. The panel can then rule at any point before 29 November, and could grant an administrative stay to buy time, deny the motions outright, or say nothing and let the deadline pass. Watch also for any DEA statement on how it will treat inventory bought before 29 November, and for state regulators in Pennsylvania, Oklahoma, Utah and Arizona telling licensees how to handle trades with businesses that missed the window.
